issues.legal_issue: An enactment included in the protective schedule is immune from invalidation under Part III whether it is inconsistent with a Part III provision or takes away or abridges a right conferred by Part III, and this immunity applies to post-constitutional as well as pre-constitutional laws.
material_facts: The challenged agricultural land ceiling legislation and its amendments were included in the protective schedule.
The challenge relied on the constitutional restriction concerning acquisition of land under personal cultivation within the applicable ceiling.
issues.conclusion: Inclusion in the protective schedule protects an enactment from invalidation on either ground, including a challenge based on the second proviso concerning land under personal cultivation.
issues.legal_principle: The broad text and purpose of Article 31B protect scheduled enactments from invalidation for inconsistency with, or taking away or abridging rights conferred by, any provision in Part III. Its wording applies to both pre-constitutional and post-constitutional legislation. The Court followed Hasmukhlal Dayabhai v. State of Gujarat.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party brings a constitutional challenge to legislation imposing limits on agricultural land holdings.
predicates.law_in_protective_schedule: The challenged enactment is included in a constitutional schedule that gives listed enactments protection from certain constitutional challenges.
predicates.challenge_based_on_part_three: The challenge alleges inconsistency with, or infringement of a right conferred by, the constitutional provisions concerning fundamental rights.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge to agricultural land reform legislation rests on Part III and the law is listed for protection, the law is immune from invalidation on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional restriction on acquiring personally cultivated land within the applicable ceiling without market-value compensation confers a fundamental property right on the holder.
material_facts: The constitutional provision barred acquisition of land under a person's personal cultivation within the ceiling applicable to that person unless the law provided compensation of at least market value.
The provision was framed as a restriction on the State's power to legislate.
issues.conclusion: The restriction is the measure of a corresponding fundamental right to market-value compensation for qualifying land.
issues.legal_principle: A limitation on State power and the corresponding guarantee to an individual are complementary aspects of a fundamental right. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh and R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, and held that the negative language and placement as a proviso did not prevent the provision from conferring a right.

predicates.constitutional_interpretation_of_propert: A court is interpreting a constitutional guarantee governing the acquisition of property by the State.
predicates.state_acquires_personally_cultivated_lan: The State acquires land that a holder cultivates personally.
predicates.land_within_holder_ceiling: The acquired land is within the ceiling applicable to that holder.

issues.definition: When the State acquires personally cultivated land within the holder's ceiling, the holder has a fundamental right to compensation at market value.

issues.legal_issue: Treating a defined family as the ceiling unit and aggregating its members' lands does not conflict with the constitutional protection for land within the ceiling applicable to a person.
material_facts: The legislation defined a family unit consisting of a person, spouse, and specified minor children.
It aggregated land held by each family-unit member, jointly or separately, and deemed the aggregate to be held by the family unit.
The ceiling was applied to the family unit, rather than separately to each individual member of that unit.
The legislation aimed, among other things, to prevent avoidance of ceiling limits through transfers to close relatives.
issues.conclusion: The family-unit provisions did not violate the constitutional restriction because the applicable ceiling in such a case was that of the family unit, not that of an individual member.
issues.legal_principle: The constitutional restriction applies where the land is personally cultivated and is within the ceiling applicable to the person whose land is acquired. When the statute makes the family unit the ceiling unit, an individual member is not separately treated as the unit for applying that ceiling. The Court also relied on the legislative purpose of preventing evasion of ceiling laws through transfers to close relatives and on Hasmukhlal Dayabhai v. State of Gujarat.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_family_unit_: A party challenges the constitutionality of agricultural land ceiling legislation that uses a family as a unit.
predicates.law_aggregates_family_members_land: The legislation combines land held separately or jointly by members of a defined family and treats it as held by that family.
predicates.ceiling_applies_to_family_unit: The legislation applies the ceiling to the family unit rather than separately to each member of that unit.
predicates.land_taken_as_surplus_over_family_ceilin: Land is taken because the aggregate holding exceeds the ceiling applicable to the family unit.

issues.definition: Where a family-unit ceiling law aggregates members' land and takes land exceeding the family ceiling, the use of that family unit does not conflict with the protection tied to an individual's applicable ceiling.

issues.legal_issue: An express constitutional amendment declaring acquisitions under a specifically identified land law void in certain circumstances does not establish a general exception to the immunity of all scheduled laws.
material_facts: An amendment adding enactments to the protective schedule included an explanation addressing acquisitions under one specifically identified tenancy law.
The explanation stated that acquisitions under that law, to the extent they contravened the constitutional restriction, would be void.
The appellants relied on that explanation to argue that scheduled enactments generally received no protection against such a contravention.
issues.conclusion: The explanation applied only to acquisitions under the specifically identified law and did not create a general exception to the protection otherwise afforded to scheduled enactments.
issues.legal_principle: The intention of the legislature, derived from the provision's language and context, controls over the label 'Explanation.' The specific explanation was necessary to produce its stated result for the identified law; it did not show an intention to remove protection from every scheduled enactment.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_schedule_imm: A party argues that a constitutional provision's protection for scheduled laws does not apply to a particular kind of acquisition.
predicates.amendment_expressly_addresses_one_identi: A constitutional amendment singles out one particular enactment for special treatment.
predicates.amendment_declares_contravention_acquisi: The amendment expressly declares acquisitions under that enactment void to the extent they contravene a specified constitutional restriction.

issues.definition: When an amendment expressly singles out one law and declares certain acquisitions under it void, that stated exception is confined to that law.

issues.legal_issue: A land-ceiling provision included in the protective schedule is valid against a challenge based on the constitutional restriction concerning acquisition of personally cultivated land.
material_facts: The challenged provision required certain transfers of land made after a specified date to be ignored when determining the ceiling and surplus area.
The High Court held that the provision violated the constitutional restriction concerning personally cultivated land within the applicable ceiling.
The enactment and its amendments were included in the protective schedule.
issues.conclusion: The provision was valid because its inclusion in the protective schedule immunised it from invalidation on that ground, even if it contravened the constitutional restriction.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B protects a scheduled enactment from invalidation for inconsistency with, or infringement of a right under, Part III. The Court applied its holding in the connected constitutional challenge concerning Article 31B.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: A party challenges the constitutionality of a provision used to determine land ceilings or surplus land.
predicates.provision_in_protective_schedule: The challenged provision is part of an enactment included in a constitutional schedule that protects listed enactments from certain challenges.
predicates.challenge_based_on_part_three: The challenge alleges inconsistency with, or infringement of a right conferred by, the constitutional provisions concerning fundamental rights.

issues.definition: A land-ceiling provision in a protected scheduled enactment remains valid against a challenge based on Part III.

issues.legal_issue: A land-reform law added to the protective schedule after a judgment declaring provisions invalid is entitled to the schedule's immunity.
material_facts: A High Court had declared certain provisions of a land-reform enactment unconstitutional under the constitutional restriction concerning personally cultivated land.
The enactment was subsequently added to the protective schedule.
The later inclusion was relied on in an appeal from the High Court decision.
issues.conclusion: The later inclusion entitled the enactment to the immunity conferred by the protective schedule, and the challenged provisions did not suffer from the alleged constitutional infirmity.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that scheduled enactments are not to be deemed void or ever to have become void on the specified Part III grounds, notwithstanding a contrary court judgment. The Court applied Hasmukhlal Dayabhai v. State of Gujarat.

predicates.challenge_based_on_part_three: The invalidation rests on inconsistency with, or infringement of a right conferred by, the constitutional provisions concerning fundamental rights.
